meta.blurb: A printer writes to a young man who is starting a business. In a few plain pages, Benjamin Franklin explains why time is money, why credit is a treasure, and why small habits decide who succeeds.
meta.bible: Benjamin Franklin: a printer of Philadelphia and the author; he wrote this essay in 1748 as an older tradesman advising a younger one; it is in the public domain and retold here in new words. The young tradesman: the reader's stand-in, a young man opening his first shop. Money of the time: twelve Pence make one Shilling and twenty Shillings make one Pound; a Crown is worth five shillings; a Groat is four pence; sixpence is half a shilling. Key ideas: Credit, Industry, Frugality, Punctuality, Honesty, Capital. Franklin's own examples: a workman who earns ten shillings a day and idles half a day; money that breeds more money; a breeding sow; a crown; a groat a day equals six pounds a year, the price for the use of one hundred pounds; the hammer heard at five in the morning and the billiard table. The imagined baker and miller are an illustration added in this retelling. Voice and tone: plain, practical and quietly witty, an old tradesman speaking to a young one; no invented quotes.

One day he leaves work at noon, and he spends only a few pence.

A man with good credit can borrow money when he needs it.
When a friend waits for his money, you can use it in the meantime.

Money can make more money, and that new money makes more.
Five shillings can become six shillings, then seven, and then still more.
With more money, each turn brings more profit than before.
A farmer who kills a mother pig loses all her future babies.

People trust a man who pays on time, and they lend to him.
A man who pays on time can borrow from all his friends.

B1B2: Benjamin Franklin is a printer who lives in the city of Philadelphia, and he has a letter to write. It is meant for a young man who is just starting his own business.
The writer speaks as an old tradesman who has learned many lessons the hard way. He hopes that a young man will gain from them without paying the same price.
To follow the advice, you need to know the money of the time. There were twelve pence in a shilling and twenty shillings in a pound.
Franklin begins with his best-known sentence, which tells the young man to remember that time is money. Every hour has a value, because an hour of work can earn something.
Franklin asks us to picture a man who can earn ten shillings a day by his work. That is what his full day of labour is worth, and it shows how valuable each hour is.
Now imagine that he spends half of one day out having a good time, or just sitting idle. He pays only sixpence for his fun, so it seems that he has lost very little.
Franklin says that the sixpence is not the only cost. The man has really thrown away five shillings more, which is the pay he could have earned in those hours.
The lesson is not that rest is wrong, but that idle hours are never free. Before you spend an afternoon, ask what that time could have earned for you.
Franklin's second lesson is just as short and just as famous, because he says that credit is money. Credit means that other people trust you enough to let you use what belongs to them.
If people believe that you will pay, they are glad to lend you money. This means that a trusted man has more to work with than he owns.
Suppose a friend lets you keep his money for a while after the day it was due. During that time you can use it to earn something, and the earnings are yours to keep.
A man with large credit who uses it wisely can make a great deal of money. His good name is working for him even while he sleeps.
Franklin says that money has a natural power to produce more of itself. A coin can make more coins, and those coins can make still more.
Franklin gives a simple example of how this works, using only a few shillings. Five shillings turned in trade becomes six, then seven and three pence, and so on until it becomes a hundred pounds.
The more money there is, the more it produces every time it is turned. For this reason, a small sum that is left to grow can become a large one.
Franklin offers a vivid scene from the farm, and it is easy to remember. A man who kills a breeding sow destroys all of her offspring, down to the thousandth generation.
In the same way, he says, a man who wastes a crown destroys everything it might have produced. A crown is only five shillings, but over time it could have become scores of pounds.
So the true price of a purchase is not only the number on the label. It is also everything that the same money could have grown into.
Franklin quotes an old saying, which is that the good paymaster is lord of another man's purse. Someone who always pays when he promised will find that other people's money is open to him.
Franklin says that a man who is known to pay exactly on time can borrow all the money his friends can spare. That can be very useful at the moments when it matters most.
Imagine a baker who gets a very large order but has little money for flour. The miller knows that the baker always pays on time, so he agrees to wait.
Franklin says that after hard work and careful saving, nothing helps a young man more than being punctual and fair. These two habits should be part of every deal he makes.
Franklin gives the young man a very strict rule about any money that he has borrowed. He must never keep it for even one hour longer than the time he promised.
If you keep the money too long, your friend will be disappointed with you. Then he may close his purse to you for ever.
Franklin reminds the young man that even the smallest actions are worth watching. Anything that touches his credit matters, however small it seems.
The man you owe may hear your hammer at five in the morning, or at eight at night. That sound makes him feel easy about his money for six months more.
But suppose he sees you at a billiard table, or hears your voice in a tavern, when you ought to be at work. The next day he will send for his money.
Franklin's point is that people judge us by what they see us do every day. Our habits are a kind of advertisement, and they speak for us whether we like it or not.
Franklin gives a second warning to people who have good credit. They are tempted to think that everything they possess is their own, and to live as if it were.
Borrowed money must always be paid back, and so it is never truly yours. A man who forgets this will spend more than he can afford.
To prevent this mistake, Franklin says that you should keep an exact account for some time. Write down what you spend and what you earn.
At first it takes some trouble to write down every small detail. Franklin says that the trouble is worth it, because of what you will learn.
You will discover how wonderfully small expenses can add up to large sums. A few coins here and there may be costing you much more than you think.
The accounts also show you what you could have saved, and what you can save in future. Franklin says that this can be done without any great inconvenience.
In short, Franklin says, the way to wealth is as plain as the way to market. Anyone who wants it can find the road, if he is willing to walk it.
Franklin says that the road depends mainly on two words, Industry and Frugality. Industry means hard work, and frugality means careful spending.
To be industrious is to waste no time at all. Every hour should be used for something that is worth doing.
To be frugal means that you waste no money at all, even in small things. A frugal person spends only on what is useful, and keeps the rest.
Franklin sums up his whole rule in one sentence. A man who earns all he can honestly, and saves all he earns, apart from necessary expenses, will certainly become rich.
The word honestly is very important in Franklin's rule. Money gained by tricks or by cheating does not belong to his plan at all.
Franklin turns to a small coin called a groat, which was worth four pence. A man who idly spends a groat every day spends more than six pounds in a year.
Franklin then makes a comparison that is easy to follow. Six pounds a year is the price for the use of one hundred pounds, so the wasted groat equals that cost.
The same lesson applies to time as well as to money, says Franklin. A man who wastes a groat's worth of his time every day loses the chance of using one hundred pounds.
Franklin adds that for six pounds a year you may have the use of one hundred pounds. The condition is that you must be known as a man of prudence and honesty.
Franklin says that whoever loses five shillings loses more than that sum. He also loses all the gains it could have made, and by old age they can be large.
Franklin ends his main argument with a note of humility, which is easy to miss. He says that the promise holds unless the Being who governs the world, in his wisdom, decides otherwise.
Franklin does not ask the young man to go without what he needs. His rule says clearly that necessary expenses are excepted.
Together, the lessons make a short list that a young man can remember. Time is money, credit is money, punctuality builds trust, and a good account book shows the truth.
Franklin's essay was printed in his own time and has been printed many times since. The words time is money are still used all over the world today.
Franklin's message is simple, and you can start on it today. Guard your hours, keep every promise, count your money, and let your daily work speak for you.
C1C2: In the year seventeen forty-eight, Benjamin Franklin, a busy printer in the city of Philadelphia, sat down to write a short essay of advice for a young man who was just opening his first shop. He wrote it as an older tradesman speaking to a younger one, in plain words that anyone could follow. Nearly three centuries later, its best-known sentences are still quoted by people who have never heard of the printer.

The essay speaks in the voice of an old tradesman, someone who has made his share of mistakes and has watched many others make theirs. He offers the young man a handful of simple rules, hoping that they will spare him years of expensive experience. Each rule, as we shall see, rests on one stubborn idea about the way a trade really works.

Franklin counts in pounds, shillings and pence, as people did in his day, so it helps to know the sums behind his words. Twelve pence made a shilling, twenty shillings made a pound, and a coin called a crown was worth five shillings, which is a quarter of a pound. When he speaks of a groat, he means a small silver coin worth four pence.

Franklin opens with the words that made the essay famous, which tell the young man to remember that time is money. It is a plain sentence, but it changes the way a person looks at a clock. From that moment, an hour is no longer an empty stretch of the day, but something that could earn, or that could be lost.

To prove his point, Franklin asks us to imagine a workman whose labour earns him ten shillings on a full day. If his whole day is worth that sum, then each hour of it has a price, and the price is easy to work out. The trouble, Franklin warns, is that most people never stop to do this simple sum for themselves.

Now suppose that he spends half the day away from his work, either enjoying himself or doing nothing at all. His entertainment costs him only sixpence, and most people would say that this is all the day has cost him. Franklin strongly disagrees with that easy answer, and he is about to explain exactly why.

The sixpence, Franklin insists, should not be counted as the only expense of that idle afternoon. The man has also thrown away five shillings besides, which is exactly what half a day of his work would have earned. The true cost of his pleasure is the money he spent and the money he failed to make.

The lesson is not that a man must never rest, but that no hour is ever truly free. Whenever we give time away, we also give away whatever that time might have earned, and this second cost is the one that nobody sees. A careful tradesman, Franklin suggests, learns to see it before he spends the hour, and not afterwards.

Franklin's second lesson is as short as the first, and it tells the young man that credit is money. Credit is the trust that other people place in you, the belief that you will pay what you owe when the day comes. Like a coin in the pocket, that trust can be spent, but it can also be lost in a moment.

When people believe that a man will repay his debts, they are willing to lend him what he needs, and their willingness is a kind of wealth. A trusted tradesman can therefore do business on a scale that his own savings would never allow. Franklin wants the young man to understand that his good name is a real part of his capital.

Franklin points out that if a man allows his money to remain in your hands after it is due, he is giving you a gift. You may use it to earn whatever profit you can during that time, and the earnings are yours to keep. For someone with large credit and good judgement, such gifts can add up to a great deal.

Where a tradesman has wide credit and the sense to use it well, the gains can be considerable, as Franklin observes. Many people never see this, because credit is something they cannot hold in their hands or count in a drawer. The man who understands it, however, treats his reputation with the same care as his savings.

According to Franklin, money is of a breeding nature, which means that it can produce more money, and its offspring can produce more again. The idea sounds strange until we remember that a sum put to work in trade comes back with a profit. Then the profit can be put to work as well, and the process continues.

Franklin offers a small example with plain numbers to make the idea clear to everyone. Five shillings, when it is put to work and turned in trade, becomes six; turned again, it becomes seven shillings and three pence, and so it goes on, round after round, until at last it has become a hundred pounds. Nothing in this is magic, and each step is small, but the steps keep adding to one another.

Franklin notes that the more money a man has, the more it produces each time it is turned, so the profit climbs faster as the sum grows. A small amount that is kept busy for many years may therefore end up far larger than anyone expected at the start. The secret lies in giving each round of profit the chance to earn more profit in its turn.

To fix the idea in the reader's mind, Franklin turns to a scene from the farm, where a man who kills a breeding sow destroys not only the animal but every pig she would ever have produced. By his own cheerful exaggeration, the loss extends all the way down to the thousandth generation. The image is a little comic and a little shocking, and it is meant to be remembered.

In the same spirit, Franklin declares that a man who wastes a crown destroys everything that the coin might have produced in the years ahead. A crown is a modest piece of money, worth only five shillings, yet properly used it could grow into many pounds. The careless spender, therefore, loses the whole future of the coin along with the coin itself.

This leads Franklin's reader to a new way of judging any purchase, for the true price of a thing is not only the sum written on its label. It is also the larger sum that the same coins might have grown into if they had been put to work. A thoughtful tradesman learns to ask that second question every time he reaches for his purse.

Franklin reminds the young man of an old saying, which declares that the good paymaster is lord of another man's purse. A man who has always paid what he owed, and paid it on the day he promised, will find that doors and drawers open for him with very little persuasion. His reputation, once it is built, works on his behalf in rooms that he never enters.

A man who is known to pay punctually, and exactly at the time he has promised, may at any moment raise all the money that his friends are able to spare, Franklin tells us. This is no small advantage, for in business the hour when money is needed rarely comes at a convenient time. The young tradesman who has earned this reputation has, in effect, an extra purse that he can open in a crisis.

To see the idea at work, imagine a baker who receives a large order just before a holiday but has little money to buy flour. The miller, who has watched him pay every bill on the promised day, hands over the sacks without a second thought. Had the baker been late even twice, the same miller might have asked to see the coins on the table first.

After industry and thrift, Franklin writes, nothing does more to raise a young man in the world than punctuality and justice in all of his dealings. These are not glamorous qualities, and they win no prizes in the moment, but they are the ones that other people remember. Over the years, such quiet memories become the solid foundation on which a good name is built.

Franklin's rule about borrowed money is severe, because it forbids the young tradesman to keep it for a single hour beyond the time he promised. He may feel that a short delay is harmless, especially when the lender is a friend and no one is in a hurry. Franklin knows, however, that promises are only believed when they are kept to the letter.

If you keep the money too long, Franklin warns, you may disappoint your friend so badly that his purse is closed to you for ever. It will not matter then how good your reasons were or how sorry you are, because trust, once it is broken, mends very slowly. A single careless week, in other words, can undo the patient work of many careful years.

Franklin now turns to something that many young people overlook, which is that the most trifling actions can affect a man's credit. People rarely read our accounts, but they all watch our behaviour, and from it they decide what kind of person we are. In a busy town, a reputation is built or lost in plain sight of every neighbour.

If the man to whom you owe money hears your hammer at five in the morning, or still ringing at eight at night, he is comforted. The sound tells him, better than any promise, that you are a person who works, and he will be content to wait another six months. Franklin knows that diligence which can be heard is worth more than diligence that is only claimed.

Suppose, instead, that the same man sees you at a billiard table, or hears your voice in a tavern, at an hour when you ought to be at work. Without waiting to ask for an explanation, he will send to collect his money the very next day. A single evening of careless pleasure, seen by the wrong pair of eyes, can undo months of patient labour.

The lesson of the hammer and the billiard table is that people judge us by what they see us do every day, and not by what we say about ourselves. Our habits are a kind of advertisement, and they speak for us whether we are present or not. A young tradesman who understands this will take care that his ordinary days tell the story he wants told.

Franklin has a further warning for people who enjoy good credit, since many of them fall into the same mistake. They begin to think that everything they possess is truly their own, and they live accordingly, forgetting that part of it belongs to those who lent it. The error is natural, because borrowed money looks exactly like any other money when it sits in a drawer.

Every coin that has been borrowed must eventually be returned, and so the borrower never truly owns it, however full his pockets may feel. A man who forgets this will spend freely until the day of repayment arrives, and then find that nothing is left. The cure, as Franklin goes on to explain, is simple, though it asks for patience.

To protect himself from this error, the young tradesman is told to keep an exact account, for some time at least, of both his expenses and his income. Every payment received and every payment made should be written down in its place. What seems like tedious work, Franklin assures him, will repay the effort many times over.

Franklin admits that it takes pains, at the beginning, to record every particular, for few people enjoy listing their pennies. Yet he assures the reader that the habit has a good effect, and he is about to say what that effect is. The work of a few weeks, he implies, can change the spending of many years.

The first discovery, according to Franklin, is how wonderfully small expenses mount up into large sums when they are written in a column and added together. A few coins spent without thought each day seem like nothing at the moment, yet in a year they may amount to a heavy sum. It is the accounts, and only the accounts, that make the invisible stream of money visible at last.

The second discovery is that the accounts reveal what might have been saved, and what may be saved in the future, without causing any great inconvenience. Many of the things we pay for, once we look at them in black and white, turn out to be things we would barely miss. Thrift, in other words, is much less painful than people imagine when they fear it.

In short, Franklin declares, the way to wealth is as plain as the way to market, a road that anyone can find who wishes to look for it. There is no secret to it, and no special talent is required, only the willingness to walk it every day. The difficulty, then, is never in knowing the way, but in keeping to it.

According to Franklin, the road depends chiefly on two words, which are Industry and Frugality, and the young tradesman is invited to carve them on his memory. Industry means hard and steady work, while frugality means a careful use of what one earns. Together they form a simple partnership that has served a great many people well.

To be industrious, in Franklin's sense, is to waste no time and to put every hour to some useful purpose. This does not demand that a man work without pause, but it does demand that he know where each hour goes. The sums of the first lesson, after all, show how much an hour is worth.

Frugality is the second word, and it means that a person wastes no money and spends only where the spending does some good. It is not meanness, for Franklin allows every necessary expense, but it is the habit of asking whether each purchase earns its place. Together with industry, it makes the best use of both of a man's treasures, his time and his money.

Franklin brings his argument to a promise, which is that the man who gets all he can honestly, and saves all that he gets, necessary expenses excepted, will certainly become rich. The promise is not a guarantee of luck, but a description of what steady habits tend to produce over a lifetime. Few of us would doubt it, yet few of us have the patience to test it.

The word honestly carries a great deal of weight in Franklin's rule, and it should not be passed over lightly. Money won by trickery or by cheating belongs to some other plan, not to his, and it would also destroy the credit on which his whole advice depends. In his view, honesty is not merely the right way to earn, but also the practical one.

Franklin chooses a small coin, the groat, which was worth four pence, to show how little it takes. A man who spends a groat every day without thought will have spent more than six pounds by the end of the year. Few people would call a groat a fortune, yet over twelve months it is a sum that no careful tradesman would ignore.

Franklin then reminds us that six pounds a year is the price paid for the use of one hundred pounds. In other words, the groat that is wasted every day equals the rent on a considerable sum of capital, which could have been working for its owner. What looked like a trivial habit turns out, on closer examination, to be a serious expense indeed.

Time, says Franklin, follows the same law as money, since he who wastes a groat's worth of it each day, on average, wastes the privilege of using one hundred pounds each day. The comparison is deliberately exaggerated, but it serves to make a plain point, which is that small daily wastes of time are never really small. They are drops that, when they are joined together, make a river of lost opportunity.

Franklin then notes that, for six pounds a year, a man may have the use of one hundred pounds, provided that he is known for prudence and honesty. The condition matters more than the price, because no sum of money can buy a reputation in a single day. It must be earned slowly, through many small and honest acts that nobody ever applauds.

Whoever loses five shillings, Franklin concludes, loses not merely that sum but every advantage that might have been made by turning it in trade. By the time a young man has grown old, those advantages may amount to a considerable fortune. The lost coin, like a seed that was never planted, takes its whole harvest with it.

Franklin, however, does not end on a note of pride, for he adds that the promise of riches holds only if the Being who governs the world does not, in his wisdom, decide otherwise. All people, he says, should look to that Being for a blessing on their honest efforts. The advice therefore combines practical confidence with a humble sense of how much lies beyond a person's control.

It would be a mistake to read Franklin as asking the young tradesman to starve himself of every comfort, for his rule plainly excepts necessary expenses. What he opposes is waste, meaning money and time that go out of the door without bringing anything good back in. Thrift, understood in this way, is not the enemy of a decent life but its servant.

Taken together, the lessons make a short list that a young tradesman could carry in his head, which says that time is money, credit is money, punctuality earns trust, and careful accounts tell the truth. Each one stands upon the others, and industry joined to frugality, he says, leads at last to wealth. That is perhaps why a letter of only a few pages has been so easy to remember.

Franklin's essay was printed in his own day, and it has been reprinted, quoted and argued over many times since. The words time is money, in particular, are now so familiar that most people who say them have no idea that they appear in a printer's letter to a young man. Few pieces of advice have ever travelled so far, and for so long, on so few words.

The advice that the old tradesman gave his young friend can be followed by anyone, in any trade, beginning this very morning. Guard your hours as carefully as you guard your coins, keep every promise to the day, record what you earn and spend, and let steady work speak on your behalf. Nothing here asks for genius, only for the quiet courage to do the plain things well, every day.
